fields.title: The Key Teachings of Gareth Evans
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of Gareth Evans’s teaching — faith as God’s work answered by obedience, hope as certain expectation, abiding in Christ, the covenant of the Upper Room, healing through forgiveness and release, every believer released to soar, and the longing for God’s manifest presence. Fourteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as an independent companion to Gareth Evans’s ministry, naming his books for the reader’s own further study.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to Gareth Evans, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus, it sets out in fourteen short chapters the teaching of a Welsh physics teacher turned pastor, ship’s chaplain and travelling Bible teacher, with a chapter on his life, a conclusion and a guide to his books. Its single thread is his conviction that in every part of the Christian life God moves first, and the believer’s part is to take His hand and walk with Him, and it weighs gently the few places where a thoughtful reader may want to read him with care.

It is important to be clear about what this book is and is not. It is an independent work of exposition, summary and appreciation. It is not written, reviewed or endorsed by Gareth Evans, and it is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by any organisation that holds rights in his writings. All descriptions of his teaching are the present author’s own summaries; his books and spoken ministry are named only for the reader’s further study, and readers are warmly encouraged to read those works themselves. Nothing of Gareth Evans’s own text is reproduced here — only Scripture, quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, and Ochorus’s account of what he taught.

His five books are his own copyright and are shared free in the Ochorus library with his permission, and eleven of his sermons, transcribed from his recorded audio, appear there by his permission as well. They are the best place to meet him.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way. Though he fall, he shall not be utterly cast down: for the LORD upholdeth him with his hand. PSALM 37:23–24

Most of the teachers in this series belong to earlier generations. Their books were finished long ago, their controversies have cooled, and the church has had time to decide what it thinks of them. Gareth Evans is different. He was born in the coal valleys of South Wales in 1938, he is still living as this book is written, and at an age when most men have long since stopped, he is still praying for his city, mentoring young believers and, by his own account, walking the streets of Victoria with people whom most churches would not know how to welcome. He is a physics teacher who became a pastor without a day at theological college, a ship’s chaplain off the coast of West Africa, and a travelling Bible teacher on five continents. He has written five books, all of them shared free in the Ochorus library with his permission, and a number of his sermons can be heard and read there too.

Why write a book of this kind about a living man? Because his books are read by people who will never meet him, in languages he does not speak. They deserve a short, honest guide to what he actually teaches, where it comes from in Scripture, and where a thoughtful reader might weigh it.

One thread through everything

Read his five books and his sermons side by side and a single conviction keeps surfacing. It is this: in every part of the Christian life God moves first, and the believer’s part is to take His hand and follow.

Evans applies that conviction to almost everything. Faith, he insists, is not something we manufacture by believing harder; it is God’s own work in the heart, answered by our obedience. Spiritual fruit is not produced by straining, as a tree does not groan its apples into being; it grows as we abide in Christ. Guidance is not a hidden blueprint we must anxiously uncover; it is a Father leading a child one step at a time, opening and closing doors along the way. Ministry is not a job the pastor hands out; it is a burden God lays on a heart and a gift He puts in a hand. Healing for wounded relationships does not begin with technique but with forgiveness, which God enables. And revival, which he has longed for since he was a young man in Wales, is not something the church can organise; it is the manifest presence of God, for which His people prepare by humility, repentance and hunger.

He has a short way of putting the thread, taken from counsel given him as a young student by an older believer in Swansea: walk with Jesus, neither running ahead of Him nor lagging behind. That picture of a walk, with the Lord setting the pace, is the best key to everything that follows.

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, drawn from the Ochorus biography and his own Stepping Stones, the book sets out his teaching in fourteen short chapters. The first six belong together: what faith is and is not, the three kinds of faith he finds in Scripture, the walk of faith as holding the Father’s hand, the neglected jewel of hope, hearing the Shepherd’s voice, and the stepping stones by which God guides. The next four turn to the believer’s life in Christ: abiding in the vine, the riches of being in Him, the fullness of the Spirit, and the covenant people of the Upper Room. Two chapters follow on his most pastoral theme, the healing of wounded relationships through dealing with offence and through forgiveness and release. The last two carry his two great burdens for the church: that every believer should be released to fly like the eagle in the ministry God intends, and that the church should seek the presence and glory of God. A conclusion draws the threads together, and a reader’s guide points you to his own books.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. That is deliberate. Evans taught physics for twenty years, and he has never lost a schoolmaster’s instinct that a lesson not practised has not been learned. He would be the first to say that nothing in these pages matters unless it sends you to your knees and then out of the door.

This is not a book by Gareth Evans but an independent summary by Ochorus. It quotes none of his words, and names his books throughout so that you can go and read him for yourself, which is the best thing to do; much of the life of his teaching lies in his stories, which a summary cannot reproduce.

Where to read with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and Evans would not want one. He is fond of pointing out that the people listed in Hebrews 11 are not heroes at all but ordinary, flawed men and women whom God led. The same must be said of the teachers who help us.

So where a thoughtful reader might want to weigh his teaching, this book says so plainly and gently. Four matters come up more than once. First, Evans draws very sharp lines between faith, hope and belief, and he builds a good deal on the Greek and Hebrew behind particular words. His pastoral point is sound and much needed, but the vocabulary of the New Testament is not always as tidy as his distinctions, and some of his word studies are disputed. Second, he loves to find pictures of Christ and the Christian life in Old Testament stories, and sometimes he reads more into a detail than the text itself requires; these readings are best taken as illustrations rather than doctrine. Third, he holds, from his Pentecostal and Alliance background, that the baptism in the Holy Spirit is a distinct experience after conversion; many faithful believers read the same passages differently. Fourth, his teaching on releasing those who have wounded us rests on a particular reading of Jesus’ words about binding, loosing and remitting sins; the heart of it, which is forgiveness, is plainly biblical, but the stories that accompany it are testimonies of God’s kindness, not promises of how every case will turn out.

None of these is a reason not to read him. The counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Where he is faithful to the Word, and on faith, obedience, abiding, forgiveness and the presence of God he is very faithful indeed, receive it gladly and act on it. Where he presses beyond what is written, set it aside and lose nothing.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before reading further, ask honestly whether you tend to run ahead of the Lord, lag behind Him, or walk with Him. Write down one recent example.

2. Decide on a pace for this book, a chapter a day or a chapter a week, and put the time in your diary now.

3. Name one area of your Christian life in which you have been trying to produce by effort what only God can give.

4. Resolve to test everything in these pages against Scripture, keeping what is true and setting aside what is not.

5. Choose one of Evans’s five books from the Reader’s Guide at the end and read its first chapter alongside the first teaching chapter here.

A PRAYER
Father, You have ordered my steps longer than I have noticed, and You have held my hand when I did not know it was held.
As I read about faith and hope, about abiding and forgiving, and about Your presence, keep me from admiring a teacher and missing his Master.
Where these pages are true to Your Word, write them on my heart. Where they are not, give me discernment to lay them down.
Keep me at Your side, Lord Jesus, neither running ahead nor falling behind, one step at a time, until the walk is done. Amen.

fields.title: From the Valleys to the Nations
fields.body_html:
Now also when I am old and grayheaded, O God, forsake me not; until I have shewed thy strength unto this generation, and thy power to every one that is to come. PSALM 71:18

A boy of the valleys. Gareth Evans was born in 1938 in Merthyr Tydfil, among the coal valleys of South Wales. His father, Cyril, served in the Royal Air Force during the Second World War and was remembered for his singing voice and his love of cricket; his mother, Ethel, was a gifted pianist who gave herself to making a home. At eight he went to live at his grandfather’s home in Bonvilston, near Cardiff, and at eleven he entered Cowbridge Grammar School, where the boy who loved cycling, football and telling stories turned out to have an unusually good head for mathematics. When he was thirteen his mother died. He did not cry at the time; boys, he had been taught, did not. His father never remarried and carried the family on his own, and the loss pressed the boy into an early independence.

A question he could not answer. He grew up in an Anglican household, familiar with the Christian faith but not yet possessed by it. At sixteen he began attending Friday-night meetings for young people run by Betty Bishop in her home, evenings of choruses, Bible quizzes and visiting speakers. One night she asked him directly what he would do with the Lord Jesus Christ. He had no answer, and for several weeks he avoided her. Then a young lay preacher he knew from school, speaking at a small chapel nearby, put exactly the same question to him after the service. That night he knelt by his bed for the first time since his mother’s death and asked Christ to forgive him and come into his life. Nothing seemed to happen. A few days later, walking into a school assembly while his friends were making fun of his new religion, he was flooded with the settled knowledge that he was a child of God. He has never doubted it since.

Teachers and a motto. He found his spiritual home in the Elim Pentecostal church at Bridgend, whose pastor, Wynne Lewis, expected young converts to follow Christ wholeheartedly or not at all. At the University of Swansea he lodged with the family of Donald Evans, a young Christian he had met on a cricket field, later a distinguished scholar of medical ethics. It was Donald’s father, Aubrey, a man with little formal education, who gave the student the counsel that became the motto of his life: that those who follow the Lord from a distance can still see Him, but those who run a step ahead of the Light of the World find themselves walking in their own shadow. From that came his resolve to walk with Jesus, neither ahead of Him nor behind. During those student years, in the spring of 1961, he also had an experience of the Holy Spirit which he has always regarded as the lighting of a fire that has never gone out.

The scientist in the classroom. He took an honours degree in physics at Swansea and a Diploma of Education. There he met Anne, a quiet young secretary in the same church, whose Norwegian father was a minister of the gospel and whose mother had been part of the prayer band associated with Rees Howells. They married in 1961. For the next two decades his pulpit was a classroom. He taught physics at Kenfig, and then, remarkably young, was appointed to teach the children of British service families in Germany, at Hamm, and later with the British forces in Hong Kong. There he joined the young Jackie Pullinger on visits into the notorious Walled City of Kowloon, and led Bible studies for British soldiers and Gurkhas. Back in Wales from 1969 he became head of physics at Ogmore Grammar School, served on a panel developing a new advanced-level curriculum, and, with Anne, saw a small Bible study for teenage girls in their home grow into a youth work across the churches of the Bridgend area. Many young people came to faith, and some of them later said that they had been living in revival without realising it.

Canada, and a school of rabbis. In 1975 the family emigrated to Canada. Evans headed the physics department at the Toronto French School and then the science department at the Toronto Hebrew Academy, an Orthodox Jewish school, where he was one of only two Gentiles on the staff. There, by invitation, he found himself answering the questions of senior students about Christ, and talking about the meaning of sacrifice with the school’s senior rabbi, conversations he counts among the high points of his life.

A teacher turned shepherd. It was in Toronto that his church’s district superintendent asked him to consider becoming a pastor with the Christian and Missionary Alliance. Evans said he would not go without a clear call from God and could not afford seminary; he was told that seminary was not required and that what was wanted was the witness of the brethren. Over the following months that witness came, unprompted, from several directions. Anne, who had grown up in the poverty of an itinerant evangelist’s home and had no wish to be a pastor’s wife, told him that if God was calling he had better obey. He left one of the best-paid teaching posts in the country for a pastor’s salary. He served first at Hazelglen Fellowship in Kitchener, Ontario, where the small congregation grew and built its own building, then briefly at Sidney on Vancouver Island, and from 1984 as pastor of Victoria Alliance Church, in the city that has been his home ever since.

Out onto the sea. In 1990 a breakdown in his ability to sleep, which his doctors attributed to stress, forced him to resign. It was a dark valley, and he later traced part of it to griefs he had never faced, going back to his mother’s death. Then came an invitation to serve with Anne as chaplains aboard the Mercy Ship Anastasis, and from 1991 to the end of 1994 they lived on board as the ship worked in West Africa. Alongside the surgery, building and clean-water projects of the ship, Evans taught pastors and church leaders, among them a series of weekly classes for over a hundred and fifty leaders in Sierra Leone, and conferences in Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal and Nigeria.

To the ends of the earth. After the ship, Anne urged him not to take another congregation but to travel and teach, while she opened their home in Victoria to students to support them. Invitations came without his seeking them: a Bible school summer school in Australia, where his teaching on the Upper Room became his first book; Youth With A Mission training schools in Mexico and Brazil; pastors’ conferences in Baja California, Haiti, India and Nepal. A long illness following surgery in 2003 kept him at home for two years, and he spent it reading, writing poetry and deepening his prayer life. Later he mentored the young founder of the SermonIndex website and helped to moderate a series of conferences on revival, and many of his sermons found listeners around the world. His books were written, he says, simply because people kept asking whether his teaching was available in print.

Holding the hand that holds tomorrow. Gareth and Anne had three daughters, and in time many grandchildren and great-grandchildren. Anne, his companion of more than sixty years, lived for many years with cancer, and died at their home in December 2025; he has written of her with deep gratitude, and gives her the credit for much that others have praised in him. In his late eighties, by his own account, he has found a new work among the addicted and homeless of Victoria, mentoring a couple who came to Christ out of that life and now serve on the streets they once knew. He describes himself simply as a worshipper, and his life as a series of stepping stones laid down by God one at a time. It is not a bad summary of what he teaches.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Trace the stepping stones of your own life. Write down three events, including at least one disappointment, through which you can now see God leading.

2. Evans came to faith because two people asked him the same direct question. Is there someone to whom you should put a simple, honest question about Christ this month?

3. Consider whether there is an old grief in your life that you have never brought to God. Ask Him, gently, to show you.

4. Anne’s willingness to follow God’s call shaped her husband’s whole ministry. Thank God by name for someone whose quiet obedience has made your service possible.

5. Ask whether you have been tempted to think your useful years are behind you. Write down one way you could still serve this generation.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You were at work in the valleys and the classrooms, on the ship and in the city streets, long before Your servant could see it. You are at work in my life in the same way.
Thank You for every stepping stone, and forgive me for the times I complained at a closed door that You shut in love.
Heal the old griefs I have buried, and make me willing to go wherever You lead, at whatever age.
Hold my hand today, and hold my tomorrows, until I see You face to face. Amen.

fields.title: What Faith Is Not
fields.body_html:
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him. HEBREWS 11:6

He Holds My Tomorrows opens not with a definition but with a wound. Evans tells of a woman he visited during a long and baffling illness, a faithful believer who could barely leave her house. One day he found her in tears. A friend from her church had telephoned to say that the prayer group had decided to stop praying for her, because if she had enough faith she would have been healed by now. Evans saw at once that something had gone badly wrong in that church’s idea of faith, and he wrote a whole book to put it right.

That opening tells you why the subject matters to him. Faith is not an abstract doctrine for Evans; it is a pastoral emergency. Wrong ideas about faith do real damage. They load the sick with guilt, push churches into foolish decisions and send disappointed believers away from God, convinced that He has failed them. Before he says what faith is, then, he clears the ground by saying what it is not.

Faith is not mere belief

The first confusion is between faith and belief. Evans does not mean that believing true things does not matter; he means that assent in the head is not the faith that saves or pleases God. James makes the point with some bluntness:

Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble. JAMES 2:19

Surveys, Evans observes, regularly show that large numbers of people in countries like Canada believe that Jesus rose from the dead. It makes no visible difference to how they live. A belief that leaves the life untouched is not what the New Testament calls faith.

He recalls how, at the Jewish school where he taught in Toronto, the senior rabbi once confided his sorrow that his students believed in God only with their heads. Evans, in He Holds My Tomorrows, turns the rabbi’s lament back on the church. Many who sit in our pews, he suggests, are exactly like those students: they have head knowledge but no living experience of Christ.

Faith is not presumption

The second confusion is between faith and presumption. Evans tells of churches, in more than one of his books and sermons, that decided to build far beyond their means because God was evidently blessing them, and branded anyone who hesitated as lacking faith. When interest rates rose and a local employer closed, the debt crushed them, people left, and many ended by blaming God. They had mistaken, in his view, a religious gamble for faith, quietly assuming that if the gamble failed the fault would be God’s.

The clearest example of the difference, for Evans, is the temptation of Jesus. Satan invites Him to turn stones into bread and to throw Himself from the temple, quoting Scripture to prove that angels will catch Him. Jesus could have done both. But to act on a promise outside the Father’s will would not have been faith; it would have been presumption.

And Jesus answering said unto him, It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. LUKE 4:12

Evans is careful here. He does not despise those who build their lives on the promises of God; he says plainly that there is much good in teaching people to stand on the Word. But he insists that we must read the Word rightly, claim only the promises that apply to us, and meet their conditions where conditions are attached. Some promises are unconditional: nothing can separate the believer from the love of God. Others, such as the peace and joy Jesus promised in the Upper Room, belong to those who keep His word.

Faith is not hope

The third confusion is one Evans returns to again and again: the confusion of faith with hope. Much of what is called faith in popular teaching, he suggests, is really hope. When a Christian says, in effect, that God has said it, he believes it and that settles it, he is expressing confident expectation of what God has promised. That is a precious thing, but it is hope. Evans sums up the distinction, in several of his books, in a simple contrast: hope belongs to the mind and shows itself in confidence; faith belongs to the heart and shows itself in obedience. He finds a hint of this in Paul’s picture of the Christian’s armour:

But let us, who are of the day, be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love; and for an helmet, the hope of salvation. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:8

The breastplate guards the heart, and it is faith and love; the helmet guards the head, and it is hope. Chapter six of this book will return to hope, which Evans thinks the church has badly neglected.

Faith is not positive thinking

The fourth confusion is with positive thinking. The business world, Evans notes, has long taught that what you think you are, you become, and much of the church has borrowed the idea. He is sharpest here about teachers who tell the sick to deny their symptoms and the poor to confess prosperity, and about the use of visualisation techniques in prayer for healing. You cannot, he says in effect, think yourself into health or into answered prayer. Such teaching is not faith, however much Scripture is quoted to support it.

Yet even here he is fair. He believes in divine healing, as the Alliance tradition in which he served has always done, and he regards healing as one of the riches won at the cross. He has himself known God to heal. But he insists that there is no formula for obtaining it, that God remains sovereign in giving it, and that no quantity of believing, praying or weeping can oblige Him. The man who cried to Jesus for his son is, for Evans, a far better model of faith than the confident claimer:

And straightway the father of the child cried out, and said with tears, Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. MARK 9:24

Weighing the distinctions

Evans’s four negatives are pastorally wise, and a great many believers have been freed by them. It is worth adding, gently, that the New Testament does not always keep the words as separate as he does. The Greek noun for faith and the verb for believe share the same root, so that in John’s Gospel to believe on Christ is simply to have faith in Him. Hope and faith are also closely woven together in Hebrews 11:1. Evans himself acknowledges that saving faith begins with believing, and his real target is not believing as such but a believing that never reaches the heart or the will. Read in that light, his distinctions are a help rather than a new vocabulary to be enforced.

The deeper point stands firm. Faith is not a quantity we generate, and its absence is not the explanation for every sorrow. No believer should ever tell a suffering brother or sister to have more faith, as though the matter lay in their hands.

Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. HEBREWS 10:38

The just live by faith; they do not live by feelings, formulas or forced confidence. What that faith is, positively, is the subject of the next chapter.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think of a time when you, or someone near you, was told that a problem was caused by lack of faith. How did it affect you? Bring that memory honestly to God.

2. Ask yourself which of the four confusions, belief without life, presumption, hope mistaken for faith, or positive thinking, you are most prone to.

3. Look back at a decision you once called a step of faith. Was it an obedient response to God, or was it presumption? What would you do differently?

4. If you know someone who is ill or struggling, resolve not to comment on the size of their faith. Visit them, pray with them, and simply be present.

5. Read Luke 4:1–13 slowly and notice how Jesus answers each temptation with Scripture rightly understood.

Lord Jesus, You refused to presume upon Your Father even when You were hungry and alone. Keep me from treating Your promises as tools for my own will.
Forgive me for the times I have confused confidence with faith, or belief in my head with trust in my heart.
Where I have wounded others by suggesting that their suffering was their own lack of faith, forgive me, and make me gentle.
I believe; help thou mine unbelief. Amen.

fields.title: Three Kinds of Faith
fields.body_html:
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. EPHESIANS 2:8–9

Having cleared away what faith is not, Evans turns to what Scripture does say about it. When he studies the Bible, he tells his readers in He Holds My Tomorrows and again in Feasting at the Table, he finds faith spoken of in three distinct ways: saving faith, the fruit of faith, and the gift of faith. The arrangement is simple, almost a schoolmaster’s outline, and that is part of its usefulness. But the conclusion he draws from it is profound, and it runs through the rest of his teaching.

Saving faith

The first kind of faith is the faith by which we are saved. Evans reads Ephesians 2:8 as teaching that even this faith is not something we supply from our own resources. We may choose to believe and want to believe, but the ability to trust Christ savingly comes from God. There is, he says in effect, no store of faith in us waiting to be tapped.

This is the faith every born-again believer shares. By it we are justified, reckoned righteous for Christ’s sake, and brought into the family of God. Evans loves to linger over grace here. He likes to set grace and mercy side by side, as many preachers have: grace lavishes on us the good we never earned, and mercy spares us the judgement we richly earned. Saving faith receives both.

Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. ROMANS 5:1

But Evans adds a sad observation, drawn from long years as a pastor. Many Christians, he believes, never progress far beyond this beginning. He finds a measuring rod for maturity in the apostle John’s address to little children, young men and fathers:

I write unto you, fathers, because ye have known him that is from the beginning. I write unto you, young men, because ye have overcome the wicked one. I write unto you, little children, because ye have known the Father. 1 JOHN 2:13

These are not ages but stages, Evans insists. He has met young believers who were already fathers and mothers in the faith, and older church members who were still children. The little child knows his sins are forgiven and can call God Father; the young man is strong, has the Word abiding in him and overcomes the evil one; the father has come to know Him who is from the beginning. Saving faith is the door, not the house.

The fruit of faith

The second kind of faith is the fruit of the Spirit. In the King James Version the list in Galatians 5 includes faith by name:

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. GALATIANS 5:22–23

Evans illustrates this with a story he has told in books and pulpits for years, and which he openly admits is invented. He and Anne, sitting in their Canadian garden one summer evening, heard a groan followed by a sigh of relief, and turned to see an apple tree straining until an apple popped out onto a branch. Then the plum trees and the cherry trees began to do the same. Nobody, of course, believes the story. Trees do not produce fruit by effort. And yet, Evans says, that is exactly how many believers think the fruit of the Spirit is produced: by trying very hard.

A tree bears fruit by standing where God planted it, drinking the rain and drawing sap from the ground. The fruit is the natural expression of the life within.

And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season; his leaf also shall not wither; and whatsoever he doeth shall prosper. PSALM 1:3

So it is with the fruit of faith. It grows slowly, over years, in the believer who abides in Christ. It requires pruning, patience and trust, but not strain. Evans adds a characteristic practical counsel: instead of constantly examining our branches for signs of fruit, we would do better to turn our eyes to the Vine.

He also notices that the fruits listed by Paul seem to become rarer as the list goes on. Most new believers taste love, joy and peace early; faith, meekness and self-control are rare and slow to ripen. And the word fruit is singular. These are not nine separate fruits but one fruit showing itself in different ways, as the one life of Christ is formed in us.

The gift of faith

The third kind of faith is one of the gifts of the Spirit listed in 1 Corinthians 12:

To another faith by the same Spirit; to another the gifts of healing by the same Spirit. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:9

Evans understands this as a special, God-given assurance for a particular situation, granted for the good of the whole body. He illustrates it with a scene he describes more than once: a church board divided over whether to employ a youth worker it cannot afford. The members pray and talk, and then one who came in opposed says that something has changed in him as he listened; he now knows the Lord is in it. Within minutes all are agreed. That, for Evans, is the gift of faith: God planting in His people, for that moment and that need, a confidence that overcomes the circumstances.

He tells too of a young friend in Wales with a crippling stammer who, against all advice, including Evans’s own, insisted on hiring a hall to tell his home town what Christ had done, and spoke clearly for the first time in his life. God had given His weak servant faith for that hour.

All from God

Having laid out the three, Evans makes the observation that governs everything else he teaches about faith. All three have their source in God, not in the believer. Saving faith is His gift; the fruit of faith is His Spirit’s growth in us; the gift of faith is His Spirit’s manifestation through us. There is nothing we can do to manufacture faith.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. HEBREWS 12:2

This is why he pleads, with some feeling, that no one should tell a sick or struggling believer to have more faith. What such a person needs to grow in, he says, is trust: the day-by-day willingness to rely on God and obey Him. That is within our reach, because it is simply the response of a child to a Father who has already acted.

Some readers will want to add that the New Testament also commands faith and commends those who grow in it; faith is God’s gift, but it is also truly our response, and Scripture does not set the two against each other. Evans would agree. His concern is with the root. Where faith is thought of as a human achievement, pride and despair follow close behind. Where it is received as God’s work, the believer is humbled and set free.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. ROMANS 10:17

The practical path, then, is not to strain after faith but to put ourselves where God gives it: in His Word, in prayer, among His people, abiding in the Vine.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Using John’s three stages, little child, young man and father, ask honestly where you are in your walk with God. Do not be discouraged by the answer; ask what the next step might be.

2. List the nine fruits of the Spirit and underline the one that seems least present in your life. Instead of resolving to try harder, spend time this week simply abiding in Christ in prayer and the Word.

3. Recall a time when you, or your church, were given an unexpected confidence that God was in something. Thank Him for it.

4. Replace the phrase have more faith in your vocabulary with an offer to pray, to help or to stay alongside.

5. Read Romans 10:17 and set aside regular time to hear the Word, not only to read it.

A PRAYER
Father, I did not find my way to You by my own believing. You opened my eyes and gave me faith to trust Your Son, and I thank You.
I confess that I have often tried to produce fruit by effort, and grown weary and ashamed. Teach me instead to abide, to drink from the river of Your Spirit, and to let You bear fruit in me in its season.
When Your people face mountains, give us faith for the hour, and let it bring glory to You alone.
Author and finisher of my faith, finish what You have begun in me. Amen.

fields.title: Holding the Father’s Hand
fields.body_html:
For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee. ISAIAH 41:13

If faith is not something we generate, what is it? Evans’s answer, given in He Holds My Tomorrows, in Stepping Stones and in his sermon on faith, is one of the most distinctive things he teaches. Faith, as he defines it, is God Himself touching the human heart and stirring it towards His will. The initiative is always God’s; the answering obedience is ours. So faith is seen, not in how strongly we believe, but in how we respond.

Evans ties all this to the meek, whom Jesus called blessed. Meekness is not weakness but teachableness, clay yielding to the potter’s hand. fields.title: The Hope of His Calling
fields.body_html:
Which hope we have as an anchor of the soul, both sure and stedfast, and which entereth into that within the veil. HEBREWS 6:19

Evans is convinced that the church speaks far too little about hope. He says so in Feasting at the Table, in He Holds My Tomorrows and in a series of sermons on Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 1. Faith is preached about constantly, and love at least sometimes, but hope, the third of Paul’s three great jewels, is rarely given its due. Evans thinks he knows why. We have let the world’s idea of hope replace the Bible’s.

The world’s hope and the Christian’s

In everyday English, Evans points out, hope always carries a shadow of doubt. We hope it will not rain tomorrow, but it may. A student hopes to pass his examinations, but he may fail. We wish a couple well on their wedding day and hope they will be happy, knowing that marriages sometimes break. The word expresses a wish with a possibility of disappointment attached.

Christian hope, he insists, has no such shadow. He describes it as a longing expectation of something already sure. The child waiting for a birthday present is his favourite picture: the child does not know what is inside the wrapping, but has no doubt at all that the gift is coming. The waiting is full of longing, not of anxiety.

And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us. ROMANS 5:5

Such hope does not disappoint, because it rests not on our wishes but on God’s promises and on what He has already done.

Paul on trial for hope

Evans’s favourite illustration of hope is Paul standing before governors and kings. Brought before the Jewish council, before Felix and later before Agrippa, the apostle does not defend himself chiefly as a man who believes certain doctrines. He says that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection.

And now I stand and am judged for the hope of the promise made of God unto our fathers. ACTS 26:6

Paul was not saying, Evans notes, that he hoped there might be a resurrection and that he had not thrown away a promising career for nothing. He was saying that he knew. His hope was a settled certainty, and it made him bold before men who could have had him killed.

That certainty rests on the resurrection of Christ. In He Holds My Tomorrows Evans sets out, in a teacher’s orderly way, why he regards the resurrection as one of the best attested events in history: the empty tomb, the appearances to many witnesses at once, and the willingness of the apostles to die rather than deny what they had seen. The whole of Christian hope, he argues, stands or falls with that one event. He finds it foreshadowed even in the brief record of Enoch, who walked with God and was not, for God took him.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, which according to his abundant mercy hath begotten us again unto a lively hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. 1 PETER 1:3

The helmet of the mind

As chapter three noted, Evans distinguishes hope from faith by placing it in the mind. Faith and love are a breastplate over the heart; hope is a helmet on the head. Hope, he says, shows itself in confidence. That is why he connects it with the exhortation in Hebrews not to throw away our confidence:

Cast not away therefore your confidence, which hath great recompence of reward. HEBREWS 10:35

Many believers, Evans observes, lack exactly this confidence. They are uncertain of their salvation, anxious about their standing with God, unsure whether heaven is really theirs. He wants them to be able to say, as he likes to put it, that they know beyond any doubt. He points to John’s purpose in writing his first letter: that those who believe on the name of the Son of God may know that they have eternal life. Christian assurance is not presumption. It is the proper fruit of hope.

He applies the same distinction, as we saw, to much popular teaching about claiming promises. When a believer declares that God has said something and so it will surely come to pass, Evans suggests, that believer is exercising hope, and there is nothing wrong with that as long as it is called by its right name and rests on promises that truly apply. The confusion comes when this confidence of the mind is called faith and then used as a lever to move God.

What we hope for

What, then, does the Christian hope for? Evans’s answer, drawn from Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 1, is breathtaking. We hope for resurrection and for being with Christ. But we also hope for the full enjoyment of an inheritance so great that Paul can only call it unsearchable.

The eyes of your understanding being enlightened; that ye may know what is the hope of his calling, and what the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints. EPHESIANS 1:18

In a sermon on this verse, Evans asks what Christ Himself has inherited: the name above every name, the keys of death and hell, the throne, and the worship of heaven. Then he adds that Christ’s inheritance is not yet complete. It will be complete in His bride, the church, the saints. We are part of His inheritance, and we are joint heirs with Him of all that is His. The Spirit given to us now is the pledge, the first instalment, of that inheritance.

The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: and if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ; if so be that we suffer with him, that we may be also glorified together. ROMANS 8:16–17

This is why Evans can speak of hope as something to be enjoyed now and not only later. The believer who knows what awaits him lives differently today. He holds this world loosely, like the patriarchs who confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. He can face illness, loss and old age with peace. Evans has spoken, with restraint, of meeting serious illness in his own home and finding there a peace he could only explain as the gift of God.

A caution and an encouragement

A careful reader may want to hold Evans’s placement of hope in the mind and faith in the heart a little loosely. Scripture speaks of believing with the heart (Romans 10:10) and of a heart that hopes, and the images of breastplate and helmet are not meant as a map of the soul. But his main point is precious and needed. Christian hope is not wishful thinking. It is an anchor fastened within the veil, in the very presence of God, where Christ has gone before us.

Now the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, that ye may abound in hope, through the power of the Holy Ghost. ROMANS 15:13
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Notice this week how often you use the word hope with a shadow of doubt in it. Ask what it would mean to hope as the New Testament does.

2. Write out Romans 8:16–17 and read it each morning for a week. Thank God that you are His heir.

3. If you are uncertain of your salvation, read 1 John 5:10–13 slowly and bring your doubts to God. Talk with a mature believer about them.

4. Consider what you would say if, like Paul, you were asked to give an account of the hope that is in you. Write a short answer, in plain words.

5. Name one fear about the future that hope in Christ addresses, and pray about it by name.

A PRAYER
God of hope, You have begotten me again to a living hope by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead. Let that hope be an anchor to my soul when the waves rise.
Open the eyes of my understanding, that I may know the hope of Your calling and the riches of Your inheritance in the saints.
Keep me from throwing away my confidence. Where I am anxious about my standing with You, let Your Spirit bear witness with my spirit that I am Your child.
Fill me with joy and peace in believing, until I see Your face. Amen.

fields.title: My Sheep Hear My Voice
fields.body_html:
My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. JOHN 10:27

If faith is a heart responding to the moving of God, then the believer must learn to recognise when God is moving. Evans gives a whole chapter of He Holds My Tomorrows to hearing God’s voice, and the theme runs through his sermons. His teaching here is a careful balance. On one side he insists that God does speak and that His sheep should expect to hear Him. On the other he is openly sceptical of much that passes for hearing God, and he warns against the damage it does.

Would it be easier with a voice from the bush?

He begins with Moses at the burning bush and asks the question most of us have asked. Would it not be easy to walk in God’s will if He spoke to us in an audible voice, as He spoke to Moses? Evans’s answer is surprising. Perhaps not. If we heard God as clearly as that, we would have no excuse at all for disobedience, and our obedience might be the obedience of fear rather than of love. God, he says, has never compelled or manipulated His people. He looks for people in whom obedience has become second nature, who obey because they love Him and want to.

And after the earthquake a fire; but the LORD was not in the fire: and after the fire a still small voice. 1 KINGS 19:12

That is why He usually speaks, not in wind, earthquake or fire, but in a still small voice that can be heard only by a soul in tune with Him. Elijah, exhausted and afraid, was not restored by a display of power but by that quiet voice. Evans adds a gentle twist to Jesus’ words to Thomas. Jesus pronounced a blessing on those who believe without seeing; the same blessing, Evans suggests, rests on those who obey without ever hearing God aloud.

Why we do not hear

If God is speaking, why do so many of His sheep not hear? Evans’s answer is that His voice is drowned by the noise of other voices. He admits that this is true of himself. He believes God speaks to him every day, but the din of his own thoughts, the world’s demands and the church’s busyness often crowd Him out.

He draws, unusually for an evangelical of his background, on the Desert Fathers, who withdrew from a newly respectable Christendom to seek God in the silence of the desert. He does not think we must become monks. But he thinks we must recover what they knew: that stillness, inner silence and time are needed if we are to recognise God’s voice. God speaks, he says, not chiefly to the intellect but to the spirit, where His Spirit communicates with ours. No degree is required, only a heart that is listening.

Yet Evans is no enthusiast for every claim to divine guidance. He confesses that few things disconcert a pastor more than a conversation that begins with someone announcing that the Lord has told them something, as though that closes the matter before counsel can begin. Evans is equally careful about prophecy. Rare moments

Evans does not pretend that God never speaks in unusual ways. He tells of a few rare occasions when he heard what he can only describe as an audible voice, always at a time of heaviness rather than spiritual achievement. He is careful to add that such experiences are rare, that they did not make him more spiritual, and that his trust in God is not built on them. It is built on the daily confidence that God leads him as he keeps hold of His hand.

The most distinctive part of Evans’s teaching on this subject concerns listening as a church. fields.body_html:
Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths. PROVERBS 3:5–6

Stepping Stones is Evans’s own story, but it is also a book of teaching. He wrote it, he explains at the outset, not simply to recount a life but to introduce readers to a God who leads His children, one step at a time, into an intimate walk with Himself. Looking back over his life he sees a series of stations, each one a place where God intervened in his plans, each leading to the next. From that long view he draws a theology of guidance that is warm, practical and, for many anxious believers, deeply freeing.

No hidden blueprint

The heart of it is simple. Evans does not believe that God keeps His will for our lives in a secret plan filed away in heaven, which we must decode by hours of anxious prayer for fear of missing it and forfeiting His favour. A loving Father, he insists, does not torment His children by hiding what He wants of them. He expects us to walk in the will He has already revealed in Scripture, and He leads us in His particular will for our lives through circumstances and the doors He opens and closes before us.

The steps of a good man are ordered by the LORD: and he delighteth in his way. PSALM 37:23

Our part, then, is not to search out a hidden path but to keep hold of His hand and walk in obedience to what we already know. Evans sums up his own attitude in a prayer he has prayed, he says, for most of his adult life: asking to be kept in God’s will to the end of the journey, admitting that he will sometimes wander from it, and inviting God to bring him back whenever he does. He asks not for a map of the road, only to be kept on it.

Disappointments and appointments

The most characteristic feature of the book is the way Evans reads his disappointments. Again and again a door he expected to open closed in his face. A teaching post in Canada was offered and then withdrawn at the last moment, leaving him embarrassed in front of friends to whom he had spoken freely of God’s goodness. A plan to move to California fell apart when a government policy changed. A request for leave to study for a master’s degree was refused.

Only years later could he see what God had been doing. The withdrawn post led to Hong Kong and to friendships that shaped his future; the collapse of later plans led, step by step, to a Jewish school in Toronto where he was given unusual freedom to speak of Christ, and from there to the pastorate. Chance meetings in wrong buildings, a single letter arriving on a particular morning, a stranger stopping his car at a roadside in India: Evans has a great many such stories, and he refuses to call them coincidences. The setbacks that grieved him most turned out, time after time, to be God’s own arrangements.

And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose. ROMANS 8:28

He is honest that this is a view from hindsight. In the moment, he questioned God, felt foolish, and needed time to yield. It took him ten years, in one case, to see why a door had been shut. The lesson is not that believers should feel no disappointment, but that they can trust the Father’s hand when they cannot see His purpose.

Led through others

Evans notices that God often leads His children through the decisions of other people, even people who do not know Him. Abraham, he points out in He Holds My Tomorrows, first set out from Ur of the Chaldees because his father Terah moved the family; it was only later that God spoke to him directly. In his own life, school governors, officials and an education officer who had once blocked his path all became, unknowingly, instruments of God’s leading. The Father’s hand is not shortened by the choices of employers, officials or even enemies.

But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive. GENESIS 50:20

Testing, not temptation

Evans distinguishes carefully between testing and temptation. God never tempts us to sin; that is the work of Satan using our own desires. But God does test His children, not so that He may learn something, for He knows the outcome already, but so that He may purify us. He uses the picture of ore in the furnace, heated until the dross is skimmed away and the pure metal reflects the refiner’s face.

That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire, might be found unto praise and honour and glory at the appearing of Jesus Christ. 1 PETER 1:7

He names several kinds of test. There is the test of offence, which chapter thirteen will consider. There is the test of the closed door. And there is the test of what we are asked to lay down: a gift, a relationship, a possession, even a calling. Like Abraham on Mount Moriah, we may be asked to give up what is most precious. God does this, Evans insists, not to hurt us but to free us from trusting in anything other than Him. And often, having laid something down, we are invited to take it up again, now as His. Moses threw down his shepherd’s staff and picked it up again as the rod of God.

Valleys before mountains

Perhaps the phrase most associated with Evans’s teaching on guidance is his conviction that every mountain top with God is reached through a valley. He has walked several: the long sleeplessness that ended his first pastorate in Victoria, two years of weakness after surgery, serious illness at home. Each time, as he tells it, the low ground gave way to high ground, and the darker the valley had been, the wider the view from the heights beyond it. The Mercy Ship years came straight after the first of those valleys.

Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. PSALM 23:4

He is careful not to turn this into a formula. There is no promise that every sorrow will be explained in this life, and Hebrews 11 itself ends with many who died without receiving what was promised. But the believer can walk through the valley knowing that the Father walks with him, and that nothing is wasted. Moses’ forty years tending sheep in Midian, which might have looked like a wasted life for a man trained in Pharaoh’s court, were God’s preparation for forty years of leading a nation through the wilderness.

A word of balance

Some readers, especially those who have known long and unexplained suffering, may find Evans’s many stories of providential timing hard to hear. Not every believer’s life contains such striking turns, and it would be a misreading of his books to measure our walk with God by the number of remarkable coincidences in it. Evans himself says that experience does not establish doctrine, though Scripture will be borne out in experience. The doctrine is plain enough: God orders the steps of His people, often unseen, and He is faithful in the dark as well as the light.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. List two or three closed doors in your life. For each, write what you can now see of God’s purpose, or, if you cannot yet see it, write a sentence entrusting it to Him.

2. Stop searching for a hidden blueprint. Instead, write down three things God has plainly revealed in Scripture that you should be doing now, and do them.

3. Ask whether God is asking you to lay something down. If so, lay it before Him in prayer this week.

4. If you are in a valley, tell one trusted believer about it, and ask them to walk with you in prayer.

5. Consider praying, in your own words, a prayer asking God to keep you in His will and to bring you back when you stray.

A PRAYER
Father, You have ordered my steps when I thought I was ordering them myself. Thank You for every door You opened and every door You shut.
Forgive me for sulking at closed doors, and for fearing that Your will is hidden from me. Teach me to walk in what You have shown me, and trust You for the rest.
When You ask me to lay something down, give me grace to do it, and to take it up again only as Yours.
Lead me through the valleys to the mountains You have prepared, and keep my hand in Yours all the way. Amen.

fields.title: Abide in Me
fields.body_html:
Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me. JOHN 15:4

If faith comes from God and fruit grows rather than being manufactured, the obvious question is how the believer stays in the place where God works. Evans’s answer is the one Jesus gave on the night before He died: abide in Me. He preached on John 15 in his sermon Abiding in Christ, and the theme runs through Feasting at the Table and Soar Like the Eagle.

In Him, and abiding in Him

Evans draws a distinction that many believers have found clarifying. It is one thing to be in Christ; it is another to abide in Him. Every born-again believer is in Christ, placed there by God at conversion and secure in Him. But Jesus repeatedly spoke to His followers about abiding, and the conditional form of His words, if ye abide in me, shows that it is possible to be in Christ without abiding.

He illustrates this with a homely picture from Feasting at the Table. A visitor to his home might truly say that he is sitting in Gareth’s house. But unless he accepts the invitation to stay, he cannot say that he is living there, sharing the table and the life of the household. Many Christians, Evans suggests, move back and forth between living in Christ and living in the world. They are like people with a fortune deposited in the bank who live as paupers because they never draw on it.

In a sermon on crossing the Jordan, he makes the same point from the story of Israel. When the tribes came to the edge of the promised land, two and a half of them asked to stay on the eastern side, because the land there was good for cattle. They knew God’s promises but preferred the comfortable pasture. We are called, Evans says, not merely to have God enter us, but to enter into God.

The vine and its branches

Evans notes that Jesus chose the vine deliberately. Throughout the Old Testament, Israel is pictured as God’s vine, and almost every time the picture appears the vine is failing: unfruitful, degenerate, broken down.

Return, we beseech thee, O God of hosts: look down from heaven, and behold, and visit this vine. PSALM 80:14

Against that background Jesus says, I am the true vine. Where Israel failed, He will bear fruit, and those who abide in Him will bear it with Him. A vine, Evans notes, needs heavy pruning, and its soft wood is good for nothing else, so a fruitless branch is fit only for the fire. A vine exists for one purpose: to bear fruit.

The marks of abiding

From the opening verses of John 15, Evans draws out what abiding will mean in practice.

First, it means pruning. He has no patience with a theology that promises unbroken victory. Every great man and woman of God he has read about, he says, went through much pruning before becoming fruitful. If you abide in Christ, you should expect the Father’s knife.

Second, it means fruitfulness, and specifically the fruit of the Spirit, which grows, as we saw in chapter four, not by straining but by drawing life from the Vine.

Third, it means that without Him we can do nothing. Evans applies this pointedly to churches. We can do a great deal for God in our own cleverness and with our own programmes, but without abiding there will be no lasting fruit.

Fourth, it means that His words abide in us, which Evans connects with obedience and with the walk of faith.

Fifth, it means answered prayer. The promise that we may ask what we will and it shall be done puzzles many believers, because so many prayers seem unanswered. fields.title: Feasting at the Table
fields.body_html:
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ. EPHESIANS 1:3

Ephesians is Evans’s favourite book of the Bible. His short book Feasting at the Table grew from lectures on it given at a Bible school summer school in Australia, and he returns to Paul’s prayers in Ephesians again and again in his sermons. The title captures his approach. Ephesians is a table spread with rich food, and most Christians, he believes, have hardly begun to eat.

In Him

The phrase that fills the first chapters of Ephesians is in Him, or in Christ. Evans introduces it with the story of Noah. Noah laboured for years to build the ark, but his salvation depended on one thing: going in. There was no deliverance for a man who stayed outside admiring his work. So it is with Christ. God has provided one way of escape from judgment, and we must enter into Him by faith.

Once we are in Him, God sees us there. When the Father looks at the believer, Evans says, He sees His Son rather than our sin; our guilt and shame are wrapped up in Christ. Then he walks through the blessings Paul lists. In Him we are chosen to be holy and blameless; adopted as sons, with all the rights of a natural son and, he notes, a security the natural son did not always have; accepted in the Beloved; redeemed and forgiven; shown the mystery of God’s will; given an inheritance; and sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise.

To the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved. EPHESIANS 1:6

These are all ours, Evans insists, simply because we are in Christ, not because of our maturity or effort. And yet they must be appropriated. They are theological truths that for many believers have never become experiential truths.

Who you are

This matters intensely to Evans because he has spent so much of his ministry with believers who do not know who they are. In The Key in My Hand he gives two long lists: what the believer is in Christ, and what the believer has in Christ. A child of God, a friend of Jesus, a joint heir with Christ, a new creation, a saint, a citizen of heaven, God’s workmanship; completely forgiven, sealed by the Spirit, seated in heavenly places, free from condemnation, with direct access to the Father. He offers his readers a prescription with a smile: take two of these truths each day and meditate on them, and the enemy’s fiery darts will lose their power.

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. ROMANS 8:1

In Soar Like the Eagle he links this to humility. Humility, he says, is not thinking badly of yourself; that is false humility, and it is as much a sickness as pride. True humility is seeing yourself as God sees you, neither inflating nor shrinking what He has made. Believers who know who they are in Christ are free to serve, because they have nothing to prove. He points to the moment in John 13 when Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into His hands and that He had come from God and was going to God, rose and washed His disciples’ feet. Security is the root of servanthood.

Seated, walking, standing

Like Watchman Nee, whose little book on Ephesians Evans read as a young youth leader in Wales, he sees the letter moving in three stages. First, we are seated with Christ in the heavenly places. Then we are called to walk worthy of that calling. Finally, we are called to stand against the enemy.

And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus. EPHESIANS 2:6

To be seated, Evans says, means to have ceased from our efforts to please God and to have entered His rest. To walk means to live out that position: in love, in the light, in wisdom, and filled with the Spirit. To stand means to put on the whole armour of God and hold our ground, not against people but against spiritual powers that were disarmed at the cross.

Egypt, wilderness and Canaan

Evans often uses Israel’s journey as a picture of the Christian life. Egypt is life without Christ. The crossing of the Red Sea, where the old taskmasters were cut off for ever, is conversion, sealed in baptism. The wilderness is the life of the believer who has come out of Egypt but not yet entered God’s promises. Canaan is the life of promise, of being sealed with the Spirit and seated with Christ.

He insists that Canaan is not a picture of heaven. The old hymns about crossing the Jordan into Beulah land have taught many to read it that way, but Canaan was a land of giants and battles, of Jericho and of defeat at Ai, as well as of milk and honey. It is a picture of the life God intends for His people now. Many in the church today, he believes, are living in the wilderness, fed faithfully by God with manna and quails and quite content. God is still gracious to them. But He brought Israel out of Egypt in order to bring them in.

There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. HEBREWS 4:9

Knowing Him

The goal of all this, for Evans, is not blessings but God Himself. Paul’s prayer is that we might know Him, and Evans means knowing in the full biblical sense of personal, experienced intimacy, not merely information about God.

That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give unto you the spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him. EPHESIANS 1:17

He draws a searching lesson from Moses’ request to see God’s glory. God answered that He knew Moses by name, and then proclaimed His own name, His character, to Moses. In Scripture, Evans notes, a name speaks of character. God reveals Himself, he suggests, according to what He knows of us. He asks his readers what name God would give them: Doubtful or Timorous, as in Bunyan’s allegory, or Faithful, Overcomer. He is not teaching that we earn revelation. He is saying that God entrusts more of Himself to those who have been tested and have overcome, as a father confides more to a son who has grown up.

And the LORD said unto Moses, I will do this thing also that thou hast spoken: for thou hast found grace in my sight, and I know thee by name. EXODUS 33:17

A word of balance

Evans’s scheme of stages, in John’s letter and in Israel’s journey, is a vivid teaching aid, and many have been stirred by it to press on. It is worth remembering that every believer is fully in Christ from the first day, and that the riches of Ephesians 1 belong to the weakest saint as surely as to the strongest. Evans would agree. His aim is not to divide Christians into classes but to call them to enjoy what is already theirs.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read Ephesians 1:3–14 and underline every occurrence of in Him, in whom or in Christ. Thank God for each blessing by name.

2. Choose two truths about who you are in Christ and meditate on them each day this week, especially when you feel accused.

3. Ask whether you have been living in the wilderness, content with manna. What promise of God have you never entered?

4. Consider whether your service springs from security or from a need to prove yourself. Read John 13:3–5 and ask the Lord to make you secure.

5. Pray Paul’s prayer in Ephesians 1:17–19 for yourself and for someone else by name every day this week.

A PRAYER
Father of glory, You have blessed me with every spiritual blessing in Christ, and I have lived as a pauper at a rich man’s table. Forgive me.
Open the eyes of my heart to know who I am in Your Son: chosen, adopted, accepted, forgiven, sealed and seated with Him.
Bring me out of the wilderness into the land of promise, and give me courage to face its giants in Your strength.
Above all, let me know You, and make me the kind of child to whom You are pleased to reveal Yourself. Amen.

fields.title: Power from on High
fields.body_html:
But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. ACTS 1:8

Evans came to faith in a Welsh Pentecostal church, served for years as a pastor in the Christian and Missionary Alliance, and describes himself as a conservative charismatic: one who believes that the gifts and working of the Holy Spirit are the same today as they have always been, and just as necessary. He speaks warmly of an experience of the Spirit in his student days which he regards as the lighting of a fire that has burned ever since. The fullness of the Spirit is therefore at the centre of his teaching, in Feasting at the Table, in Soar Like the Eagle and in his sermon Guard the Fire.

Breathed on, and then empowered

Evans’s starting point is the difference between two scenes in the Gospels and Acts. On the evening of the resurrection, Jesus came to His frightened disciples in a locked room, showed them His hands and side, and breathed on them.

And when he had said this, he breathed on them, and saith unto them, Receive ye the Holy Ghost. JOHN 20:22

Evans believes that at that moment the disciples were born again. He points to the form of the Greek verb, which he takes as a command expecting immediate fulfilment. But seven weeks later, at Pentecost, the same disciples were filled with the Spirit in power. In between, Jesus had told them to wait in Jerusalem.

And, behold, I send the promise of my Father upon you: but tarry ye in the city of Jerusalem, until ye be endued with power from on high. LUKE 24:49

For Evans these are two distinct works. The first is new birth, by which the Spirit baptises us into the body of Christ; the second is the baptism in the Spirit, by which the risen Lord empowers His people for witness. He uses two Greek words for power to mark the difference: the authority to become children of God in John 1:12, and the dynamic power for witness in Acts 1:8. Too many believers, he fears, live only in the first.

He finds the same pattern at Ephesus, where Paul met disciples who had believed but had not heard of the Holy Spirit, and laid hands on them.

He said unto them, Have ye received the Holy Ghost since ye believed? And they said unto him, We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost. ACTS 19:2

Even Jesus waited

His most striking argument is from the life of Christ. Jesus was conceived by the Holy Spirit and was full of the Spirit from birth. Yet He did not begin His public ministry until the Spirit descended on Him at His baptism. Then, in the synagogue at Nazareth, He read from Isaiah and declared that the Scripture was fulfilled.

The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised. LUKE 4:18

If Jesus needed the anointing of the Spirit to do the work He was sent to do, Evans asks, how much more do we?

How to receive

Evans does not teach a technique for receiving the Spirit. He speaks instead of longing and preparation. The disciples tarried, and their waiting was not idle but full of prayer, worship and expectation. Jesus’ words about asking, seeking and knocking, he notes, are all in the continuous tense: keep on asking.

If ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him? LUKE 11:13

He adds that those who would enter God’s presence must come with clean hands and a pure heart, and suggests that we might well practise the attitudes that mark a Spirit-filled life as a preparation for receiving it.

Three evidences

Those three attitudes are among the most frequently repeated points in all Evans’s teaching. When Paul tells the Ephesians to be filled with the Spirit, he at once describes what such a life looks like.

And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord; giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God. EPHESIANS 5:18–21

A worshipping heart, a thankful heart and a servant heart: these, Evans says, are the marks of fullness. He is blunt about it. A believer who does not worship, who complains habitually, or who refuses to defer to others, has in his view no business claiming to be full of the Spirit. He notes too that Paul’s instruction to be filled is in a continuing form, so that while the first filling is God’s sovereign gift, the ongoing filling is something for which we bear responsibility. And he points out that Paul places the great chapter on love between his two chapters on spiritual gifts. Gifts without love are noise.

Filling and anointing

Evans makes one further distinction. Filling, he says, is within; anointing is upon. Filling prepares us for service; anointing comes as we are released into the service God has called us to. The filling depends, over time, on our openness; the anointing remains God’s sovereign choice. He defines anointing as God putting His seal on a person or a ministry so that it has an eternal effect on those it touches. Chapter fifteen returns to this.

Gifts, with discernment

Evans believes in the gifts of the Spirit, including prophecy, words of knowledge and healing, and, as the Alliance has always taught, that healing is among the benefits of the cross; he testifies to having been healed himself. But he insists there is no formula, and he is equally firm against charismatic excess: unaccountable personal prophecies, manipulation from platforms, emotion mistaken for the Spirit’s presence. What he wants is not noise but God.

Weighing the teaching

Here a reader should know that Evans is taking a side in a long conversation among faithful Christians. Many believers, including many who long for the Spirit’s power as much as he does, read the same passages differently. They understand Pentecost as a unique moment in the history of salvation, and Ephesians 1:13 as teaching that every believer is sealed with the Spirit on believing. They see later fillings as renewed experiences of the Spirit already given, not as a second stage every Christian must seek. Evans knows this well; some of his closest friends in Victoria came from Brethren backgrounds that held the other view, and he honoured them. He is also sharper than many would be about teachers who believe the miraculous gifts have ceased.

What all can receive from him is his refusal to settle for a powerless faith. Whatever one’s view of the order of events, Scripture commands every believer to be filled with the Spirit, and the marks of that fullness, worship, thanksgiving and humble service, are open to test in any life.
