fields.body_html:
After the same manner also he took the cup, when he had supped, saying, This cup is the new testament in my blood: this do ye, as oft as ye drink it, in remembrance of me. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:25

The Key in My Hand, Evans’s first book, begins not with wounds or forgiveness but in the Upper Room. So does a whole chapter of Feasting at the Table. His reason is simple. If you knew you had only a day to live, he asks, what would you do? You would not spend it on trivial things. You would gather those you love, tell them what matters most, and put right anything between you. On the night before He died, Jesus did exactly that. He dealt with priorities.

Three requirements

Evans finds three requirements in Jesus’ words to His disciples in John 13 and 14.

The first is servanthood. The disciples arrived with dusty feet and no servant to wash them, and Jesus Himself took the towel and basin and washed their feet, including the feet of Judas, who would betray Him that night.

If I then, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet; ye also ought to wash one another’s feet. JOHN 13:14

Evans does not think Jesus meant chiefly a ritual, though he has found foot-washing services a blessing. He meant that we are to refresh one another from the dirt that clings to us from walking in this world. That, he says, is one of the chief purposes of Christian fellowship, and one reason he goes to church: to have his feet washed. The tragedy is that there is often as much dirt thrown among believers as among unbelievers.

The second is love. Jesus gave a new commandment, not an option: that we love one another as He has loved us. Liking one another, Evans observes wryly, is not commanded; loving one another is, and love rules out gossip and backbiting and makes us ready to honour and prefer others.

A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. JOHN 13:34

The third is obedience to His word. If you love me, keep my commandments.

Promises and covenant

Alongside the requirements, Jesus made promises: a place prepared in the Father’s house, His return, the Comforter, peace that the world cannot give or take away, and joy that is full. Evans points out that these promises are covenant promises. Their enjoyment depends on the disciples keeping their side: being servants, lovers and obedient.

That is why he calls this the covenant of the Upper Room. A covenant, he explains, is an agreement between two parties, and in the ancient world covenants were cut with the shedding of blood. When Jesus took the cup and called it the new covenant in His blood, the disciples, he notes, did not ask what He meant. They understood. And so, Evans says, every time we take the bread and the cup, we renew our agreement. As we eat the bread we declare that we are part of Christ’s body. As we drink the cup we covenant again to serve one another, love one another and obey His word. He describes his own habit at the Lord’s Table of looking round at the congregation as he takes the bread, and quietly renewing those three commitments as he takes the cup.

But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:28

The unity that evangelises

From the Upper Room Evans moves to Jesus’ prayer in John 17, and to what he regards as the church’s most neglected method of evangelism. You cannot, he observes, tear out a single page of the Bible and hand it to someone as a gospel tract. But you can point to whole chapters that tell us how God intends the world to believe.

That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. JOHN 17:21

When God’s people live together as servants and lovers in obedience, he says, the world will know and believe. The church’s own life together is the message God means the world to read. That is why he pleads for the church to confront its divisions and bitterness, which the world sees so clearly, as quickly as it confronts false teaching.

One body

Evans gives much space to Paul’s picture of the church as a body: not an organisation made by men but an organism made by God, into which every believer, of whatever denomination, has been baptised by one Spirit. He is not against denominations as such. But when our groupings divide us from those in Christ who differ on styles of worship or secondary interpretation, we bring condemnation on ourselves.

And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:21

The tragic truth

He is unsparing about how far the church falls short. Christian marriages that should show the world Christ’s love for His bride end in divorce as often as others do. Children raised in Christian homes carry the wounds of fathers who provoked them to anger. Business people tell him that Christians can be among the worst to deal with. Missionaries, he notes, leave the field more often through broken relationships than through illness or finance, and pastors leave churches after a few years of disappointed expectations. Churches compete for each other’s members and occasionally tear themselves apart in fights that the whole town remembers. After each example he asks, in effect, what the watching world is supposed to make of it.

He does not ask it to condemn. He asks it because he believes the enemy of our souls has made the breaking of relationships his chief strategy, precisely because unity is God’s priority. The next two chapters take up his remedy.

A caution about sickness

One part of Evans’s covenant teaching needs care. From Paul’s warning that some Corinthians were weak and sick because they took the Lord’s Supper unworthily, and from James’s instruction to call the elders, he suggests that some sickness among believers may be linked to broken relationships in the body, and that elders should discern whether reconciliation is needed before praying. He is right that Scripture makes such a link in some cases, and his pastoral concern is genuine. But the same Scripture shows that most sickness has no such cause, as Jesus said of the man born blind, and Evans himself is fierce against those who tell the sick that their illness proves some failure in them. His teaching is best received as a call to examine ourselves at the Table, never as a diagnosis to be applied to others.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Next time you take the Lord’s Supper, consciously renew the three commitments of the Upper Room: to serve, to love and to obey.

2. Think of someone in your church whose feet need washing this week, someone weary or discouraged. Do something practical to refresh them.

3. Is there a brother or sister you do not like? Ask God for grace to love them, and show that love in one concrete act.

4. Consider whether your church has made heresy of practice as serious as heresy of doctrine. Pray for unity among the churches in your town by name.

5. If you are carrying bitterness toward someone in the body, do not take the cup until you have at least begun to seek reconciliation.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, on the night You were betrayed You took a towel and washed the feet of Your friends, and of the one who would betray You. Make me a servant like You.
You have commanded me to love as You have loved me. I cannot do it without Your grace; give it to me for the people I find hardest to love.
As I eat the bread and drink the cup, let me mean what I promise: to serve Your people, to love Your people and to obey Your word.
Make us one, Lord, so that the world may believe that the Father sent You. Amen.

fields.title: The Rock of Offence
fields.body_html:
Then said he unto the disciples, It is impossible but that offences will come: but woe unto him, through whom they come! LUKE 17:1

If unity is God’s priority, Evans reasons, it must also be the enemy’s target. In The Key in My Hand he describes the devices Satan uses against believers: the roar of the lion that plays on our emotions, the fiery darts of lies aimed at our minds, and the hook of the angler cast into old wounds. But the device he writes about most, and preaches about most often, is offence. It is, he believes, the cause of more church splits, more departures of missionaries from the field and more pastors leaving the ministry than any other.

Offence is not sin

Evans begins with a distinction that surprises many readers. Offence and sin are not the same. Jesus Himself was a rock of offence, as both Paul and Peter say, and He was without sin.

And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient. 1 PETER 2:8

The Pharisees were offended at Him, His own townspeople were offended at Him, and even His family took offence. Sometimes, Evans suggests, Jesus seems to have caused offence deliberately. At other times, as with the temple tax, He took care to avoid it. Being offended is not in itself sinful. What we do with offence is another matter.

He finds this in the story of Cain. God did not reject Cain’s offering because Cain had sinned; there is nothing in the text to say his gift was wicked. But Cain was angry and his countenance fell, and God warned him that sin was crouching at the door. The offence came first; the sin followed only when Cain refused to master it.

If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him. GENESIS 4:7

What offence costs

In The Key in My Hand and again in He Holds My Tomorrows, Evans traces five Gospel examples of people who were offended, and what it cost them. The hearer on stony ground receives the word with joy but is offended when trouble comes, and bears no fruit. The people of Nazareth are offended at the carpenter’s son, and He does few mighty works there. Judas is offended at the waste of costly ointment, and goes out to betray his Master, having lost all confidence in Him. Peter is offended on the night of the arrest and denies Christ before a servant girl, losing his testimony. And many disciples, offended at Jesus’ hard sayings about eating His flesh, go back and walk no more with Him.

From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. JOHN 6:66

No fruit, no miracles, no confidence, no testimony, no fellowship: that, for Evans, is the harvest of offence nursed rather than dealt with.

Offended at Jesus

Two of his examples are especially personal. John the Baptist, in prison, waited for the cousin he had proclaimed as the Lamb of God to come and set him free. Jesus did not come. John sent to ask whether He was really the Coming One, and Jesus answered with a list of His works and a gentle warning.

And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me. MATTHEW 11:6

The second is Mary of Bethany. When Lazarus died, Martha went out to meet Jesus, but Mary stayed in the house. When she finally came, she said the same words as her sister, but Jesus answered her differently; He wept. Evans suggests that Mary had taken offence because He had not come in time, and that Jesus wept, not for Lazarus, whom He was about to raise, but because His friend was offended at Him.

This is an arresting reading, and it has helped many to see their own hurt at God’s timing in a new light. It should be said plainly, though, that it goes beyond what the text states. John tells us that Jesus wept when He saw Mary and the mourners weeping, and many readers understand His tears as compassion and grief at the ravages of death. Evans’s interpretation is best held as a possible application rather than as the meaning of the passage.

Why God allows it

Why does God allow offences to come? Evans answers that they reveal to us something about ourselves. John the Baptist had said that Christ must increase and he must decrease, but he still needed to learn that the timetable was God’s and not his. Believers are easily tempted to try to steer God into doing things their way, and to be offended when He will not. Offences are one of the ways God tests and refines us, exposing pride, false expectations and a desire for prominence.

He lists common causes: personality clashes, unspoken and unmet expectations, misunderstandings, envy of others’ gifts, wounded pride and simple rebellion.

What to do with it

Evans’s counsel, in The Key in My Hand, is simple and practical, and he frames it as a sequence. First, take responsibility for the offence: it is yours, for the other person may not have sinned at all; you are the one who picked it up. Next, learn from it: ask what God is showing you about yourself. Then let it go: choose to lay it down, pray about it, bless the one who offended you, and ask the Spirit for grace if it feels too heavy. Last, leave it behind: do not let it take up residence in your heart. And finally, take care not to be the cause of offence to others.

Looking diligently lest any man fail of the grace of God; lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled. HEBREWS 12:15

He adds a point from Matthew 18 that many find liberating. Jesus tells us to go to a brother who has sinned against us. He does not tell us to go to everyone by whom we have been offended. Many conflicts would be avoided if believers simply laid down their offences instead of confronting others over them, and many more if those who wished to leave a church did so graciously, telling their pastor rather than simply drifting away.

Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: neither give place to the devil. EPHESIANS 4:26–27

Anger and hurt are feelings, and feelings are not in themselves sinful. But unresolved, they give the devil a foothold. Evans’s counsel is to deal with them the same day.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask the Lord to show you any offence you are carrying, against a person, a church or even Him. Write it down.

2. Take that offence through Evans’s sequence: take responsibility for it, learn from it, let it go and leave it behind. Do not skip the learning.

3. Is there a place where you have been offended at God’s timing? Bring it honestly to Him, as Mary eventually came to Jesus.

4. Distinguish, in one current conflict, between being offended and being sinned against. If you have been sinned against, consider going privately, as Matthew 18:15 directs.

5. Ask whether you are causing offence to someone. If so, go and put it right.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were a rock of offence to many, and I too have stumbled when You did not act as I expected. Forgive me.
Show me the offences I have picked up and carried. Give me grace to take responsibility for them, to learn from them, to lay them down and to leave them with You.
Guard my heart from bitterness, and do not let the sun go down on my anger.
Blessed is the one who is not offended in You. Make me such a one. Amen.
fields.body_text: Then said he unto the disciples, It is impossible but that offences will come: but woe unto him, through whom they come! LUKE 17:1 If unity is God’s priority, Evans reasons, it must also be the enemy’s target. In The Key in My Hand he describes the devices Satan uses against believers: the roar of the lion that plays on our emotions, the fiery darts of lies aimed at our minds, and the hook of the angler cast into old wounds. But the device he writes about most, and preaches about most often, is offence. It is, he believes, the cause of more church splits, more departures of missionaries from the field and more pastors leaving the ministry than any other. Offence is not sin Evans begins with a distinction that surprises many readers. Offence and sin are not the same. Jesus Himself was a rock of offence, as both Paul and Peter say, and He was without sin. And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient. 1 PETER 2:8 The Pharisees were offended at Him, His own townspeople were offended at Him, and even His family took offence. Sometimes, Evans suggests, Jesus seems to have caused offence deliberately. At other times, as with the temple tax, He took care to avoid it. Being offended is not in itself sinful. What we do with offence is another matter. He finds this in the story of Cain. God did not reject Cain’s offering because Cain had sinned; there is nothing in the text to say his gift was wicked. But Cain was angry and his countenance fell, and God warned him that sin was crouching at the door. The offence came first; the sin followed only when Cain refused to master it. If thou doest well, shalt thou not be accepted? and if thou doest not well, sin lieth at the door. And unto thee shall be his desire, and thou shalt rule over him. The hearer on stony ground receives the word with joy but is offended when trouble comes, and bears no fruit. The people of Nazareth are offended at the carpenter’s son, and He does few mighty works there. Judas is offended at the waste of costly ointment, and goes out to betray his Master, having lost all confidence in Him. Peter is offended on the night of the arrest and denies Christ before a servant girl, losing his testimony. And many disciples, offended at Jesus’ hard sayings about eating His flesh, go back and walk no more with Him. From that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. JOHN 6:66 No fruit, no miracles, no confidence, no testimony, no fellowship: that, for Evans, is the harvest of offence nursed rather than dealt with. John sent to ask whether He was really the Coming One, and Jesus answered with a list of His works and a gentle warning. And blessed is he, whosoever shall not be offended in me. MATTHEW 11:6 The second is Mary of Bethany. When Lazarus died, Martha went out to meet Jesus, but Mary stayed in the house. When she finally came, she said the same words as her sister, but Jesus answered her differently; He wept. Evans suggests that Mary had taken offence because He had not come in time, and that Jesus wept, not for Lazarus, whom He was about to raise, but because His friend was offended at Him. First, take responsibility for the offence: it is yours, for the other person may not have sinned at all; you are the one who picked it up. Next, learn from it: ask what God is showing you about yourself. Then let it go: choose to lay it down, pray about it, bless the one who offended you, and ask the Spirit for grace if it feels too heavy. Last, leave it behind: do not let it take up residence in your heart. And finally, take care not to be the cause of offence to others. Many conflicts would be avoided if believers simply laid down their offences instead of confronting others over them, and many more if those who wished to leave a church did so graciously, telling their pastor rather than simply drifting away. Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: neither give place to the devil. EPHESIANS 4:26–27 Anger and hurt are feelings, and feelings are not in themselves sinful. Ask the Lord to show you any offence you are carrying, against a person, a church or even Him. Write it down. 2. Take that offence through Evans’s sequence: take responsibility for it, learn from it, let it go and leave it behind. Do not skip the learning. 3. Is there a place where you have been offended at God’s timing? Bring it honestly to Him, as Mary eventually came to Jesus. 4. Distinguish, in one current conflict, between being offended and being sinned against. If you have been sinned against, consider going privately, as Matthew 18:15 directs. 5. Ask whether you are causing offence to someone. If so, go and put it right. A PRAYER Lord Jesus, You were a rock of offence to many, and I too have stumbled when You did not act as I expected. Forgive me. Show me the offences I have picked up and carried. Give me grace to take responsibility for them, to learn from them, to lay them down and to leave them with You. Guard my heart from bitterness, and do not let the sun go down on my anger. Blessed is the one who is not offended in You. Make me such a one. Amen.

fields.title: The Key in My Hand
fields.body_html:
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you. EPHESIANS 4:32

The Key in My Hand is Evans’s best-known book, and the teaching in it has travelled further than anything else he has written. He taught it to youth groups and retired people, to liturgical congregations and free churches, to Bible colleges and men’s retreats, and he says that almost everywhere it drew an emotional response. Its subject is the healing of wounded souls and broken relationships, and its key, as the title says, is forgiveness.

A new creation, and a wounded soul

Evans begins with a question that troubled him as a young Christian. If anyone in Christ is a new creation, why do so many believers still struggle with the same fears, compulsions and hurts they carried before conversion? He had been made to feel guilty that old things had not visibly passed away.

His answer uses a simple framework of spirit, soul and body. At conversion, he says, the human spirit, once dead to God, is made alive; that is the new creation. The body is plainly not made new; it goes on ageing and will be redeemed only at the resurrection. And the soul, by which he means the mind, will and emotions, is not instantly healed either. It carries into the Christian life the wounds of the past, and those wounds become a battlefield where the enemy loves to work.

And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:23

He sees here the three tenses of salvation. Justification has saved us from the penalty of sin; sanctification is saving us from its power; glorification will save us from its presence. The healing of the soul, he suggests, is a large part of that present work of sanctification.

He describes such wounds in the language of physical injury, from the bruising of years of criticism to deep wounds of abuse that are buried, and the fractures of trauma from which some have limped ever since. He tells his own story here too, of how a long illness in 1990 led him to discover a wound of abandonment going back to his mother’s death, which he had never grieved.

He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds. PSALM 147:3

The key

What is the remedy? Evans respects good counselling and has used many Christian books on inner healing. But he is troubled that so much of it aims only at helping wounded people cope, and that so little of it speaks of the releasing power of forgiveness. The Lord, he believes, intends not merely to help us manage our wounds but to heal them, and the key is in our own hands.

He finds that key in Jesus’ words about binding and loosing. Many interpretations have been offered of Matthew 16:19, but Evans notes that Jesus repeats the words to all the disciples in Matthew 18, in a chapter wholly about restoration, reconciliation and forgiveness.

Verily I say unto you, Whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. MATTHEW 18:18

He links this with Jesus’ words to the disciples on the evening of the resurrection:

Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained. JOHN 20:23

We cannot forgive sins as God forgives them, Evans says; only God can remove sin as far as the east is from the west. But we can forgive the sins committed against us, and in doing so we can release those who wounded us from our own claim against them. He always speaks of forgiveness and release together. His great example is Stephen, who as he was stoned prayed that the Lord would not lay this sin to his murderers’ charge.

And he kneeled down, and cried with a loud voice, Lord, lay not this sin to their charge. And when he had said this, he fell asleep. ACTS 7:60

Evans wonders aloud whether Saul of Tarsus, standing by that day, would ever have become the apostle Paul had Stephen not prayed as he did. Forgiveness, he believes, opens a door through which God can reach the one who has wronged us. And it frees the one who forgives, who has been bound to the offender by the pain of the wound as surely as by a rope.

Walking out healing

Evans’s practical counsel is gentle and unhurried. He tells readers to ask the Holy Spirit to direct their thoughts, and to take their time; healing rarely comes quickly. He encourages them to talk through their past, to recognise honestly where they were wounded by another’s sin, without either blaming others for their own failings or excusing those who hurt them. He suggests writing a letter, never to be sent, setting out specifically how they were hurt and what they longed for, so that buried pain can be brought into the light. Then comes the choice to forgive each thing written, and to pray a prayer of release like Stephen’s; then to destroy the letter as a sign that the matter is settled; and then to pray daily for blessing on the one who caused the wound, and to remain open to reconciliation when it is possible.

But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you. MATTHEW 5:44

He tells a number of stories, with names changed, of people who took this path and found not only their own healing but a changed relationship with a parent or teacher who had wounded them. They are moving stories, and he tells them as testimonies to the goodness of God.

Weighing the teaching

The heart of this teaching, that believers must forgive from the heart as they have been forgiven, and that bitterness binds us while forgiveness frees us, is plainly taught throughout Scripture. Many have found freedom through it, and the church needs it urgently.

Some parts ask for care. Evans’s reading of binding, loosing and remitting sins is one of several held by faithful interpreters; others understand these words as belonging to the proclamation of the gospel and the discipline of the church, rather than to private acts of release. His stories of offenders whose hearts were changed after a prayer of release are testimonies of God’s kindness, not guarantees; some who forgive will never see the other person change, and their forgiveness is no less real. Forgiveness does not require a wounded person to return to someone who is still dangerous; reconciliation depends on repentance on both sides. And where deep trauma or abuse is involved, the help of a wise and qualified counsellor is a gift, not a failure of faith. Evans himself encourages his readers to find a good counsellor to walk with them, and warns that not every recovered memory is accurate. His purpose, he insists, is not recrimination but freedom.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask the Holy Spirit gently to show you any wound you have carried from the past. Do not rush; write down what comes.

2. If a particular person comes to mind, consider writing the kind of unsent letter Evans describes. Be specific. Take your time.

3. When you are ready, forgive each thing you have written, and pray in your own words that God would not lay those sins to that person’s charge.

4. Begin to pray daily for God’s blessing on the one who hurt you, and notice how it changes your own heart.

5. If your wound is deep, find a mature, trustworthy Christian counsellor or pastor to walk with you, and do not be ashamed to ask.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were wounded for my transgressions, and by Your stripes I am healed. You know every wound I carry, for You were there when it happened.
I bring You the hurts I have buried and the people who caused them. By Your grace I choose to forgive them, and I ask You not to lay these things to their charge.
Loose me from the bitterness that has bound me to them. Heal my soul, restore what was broken, and teach me to walk in freedom.
And make me a peacemaker, so that others may find in me the forgiveness I have found in You. Amen.

fields.title: Soar Like the Eagle
fields.body_html:
As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings: so the LORD alone did lead him. DEUTERONOMY 32:11–12

Evans has watched eagles on the islands off Vancouver Island riding the rising air with hardly a movement of their wings, and the sight has become the governing image of his book Soar Like the Eagle and of several sermons. It is God’s desire, he says, that His people should soar. Yet many believers are more like farmyard chickens, pecking contentedly at the grain of church programmes, while others have tried to fly by their own effort and crashed. The book asks why, and what can be done.

Why so few fly

Evans gives several reasons. Some believers are carrying wounds of the soul that have never been healed, the subject of the last chapter. Some have made decisions contrary to God’s principles, and he names debt and marriage to an unbeliever as examples. Some have simply never been taught that they should fly; they have settled for being fed each Sunday. And some have had their wings clipped by leaders who run the church like a business or a fiefdom, with power flowing from the top down, and who discourage any initiative that might disturb the comfortable order of things.

He is especially grieved by the last. Jesus told His disciples that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over their people, but it was not to be so among them.

But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve. LUKE 22:26

The pastor’s calling, Evans insists, is not to sit at the top of a pyramid but to serve from beneath it, equipping the saints for the work of ministry. His task is to teach them to fly, not to build ever larger nests to keep them in.

From burden to anointing

Evans draws a pattern from the story of the prophet’s widow in 2 Kings 4, whose creditors were about to take her two sons as slaves. He uses the story, he says openly, as a parable rather than an exposition. The widow could see nothing but darkness, and Evans begins with how we see: ourselves, the world and God. He is as concerned with the false humility that insists it is nothing as with pride; in a child of God, he suggests, such talk comes close to denying what God has done.

The widow also carried a heavy burden, and Evans believes God lays on each believer a particular concern that will not go away: for young people, for prisoners, for the poor, for prayer. He tells how, as a young teacher in Germany, he asked God for a burden for youth, and how years later he found himself leading a youth work that grew beyond anything he had imagined. The burden God gives is light, because it is carried in His yoke. A burden someone else lays on us is heavy.

Then the prophet asked what she had in the house.

And Elisha said unto her, What shall I do for thee? tell me, what hast thou in the house? And she said, Thine handmaid hath not any thing in the house, save a pot of oil. 2 KINGS 4:2

Every believer, Evans says, has been given the Holy Spirit and gifts by which to carry his burden, as well as natural abilities God can use: Moses had a staff, David a sling, Peter a net, Paul his Roman citizenship. The burden is something each believer must name for himself; the gift is best recognised and confirmed by others. The prophet then gave the widow a task that seemed absurd, to borrow every empty vessel and pour, and Evans believes church leaders should likewise help each member find a ministry that fits burden and gift. As she obeyed, the oil kept flowing. That, for him, is anointing: God setting His seal on obedient service, so that it bears fruit far beyond human ability, and the believer begins to soar.

Releasing the eagles

Much of the book is addressed to pastors and elders, and its counsel is practical. Evans suggests that every elders’ meeting should include two things: prayer to seek the mind of God, and a time to ask who in the congregation is ready to be released into ministry. Leaders should listen to people’s burdens, help them put them into words, seek confirmation of their gifts, and then give them room to serve, with clear authority, responsibility and accountability.

As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. 1 PETER 4:10

His stories include a man with a burden for prayer who, once released to teach it, helped a small congregation learn to wait on God and grow. Evans insists that releasing others is risky. They may fail and embarrass us; they may succeed and surpass us. Only leaders secure in their own calling can do it freely.

God’s work in God’s way

Evans returns often to the story of David bringing the ark to Jerusalem. The first attempt, on a new cart drawn by oxen, copied the method the Philistines had used, and ended in death. Only when David searched the law and had the Levites carry the ark on their shoulders, as Moses had commanded, did the presence of God come home with rejoicing.

For because ye did it not at the first, the LORD our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order. 1 CHRONICLES 15:13

The lesson, Evans says, is plain: if you want to do God’s work, do it God’s way. Much of the church, he fears, has borrowed the world’s methods of management, marketing and control, and wonders why the anointing is absent.

Weighing the teaching

Evans’s picture of the church as a place where every member is equipped and released is thoroughly biblical, and his warnings against controlling leadership are timely. Some of his applications may be weighed. His strong words about debt and about marriage to an unbeliever are pastoral warnings, not verdicts; he himself distinguishes a sensible mortgage from reckless borrowing, and Scripture is clear that God can greatly use a believer whose spouse does not yet believe. His belief that apostles and prophets are still given to the church today is held by many and questioned by others. And his confidence that God will anoint whatever is done in the right way should be held together with his own teaching that anointing is always God’s sovereign gift.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. What burden has God laid on your heart? Try to describe it in a single clear sentence.

2. Ask two mature believers what gifts they see in you, and listen carefully.

3. Consider whether you have been waiting for someone else to carry a burden God has given to you. Take one step to begin.

4. If you lead in any way, think of one person you could release into ministry this year. Talk with them about their burden.

5. Look at one area of your church’s life and ask honestly whether it is being done God’s way or the world’s.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have not made me to sit in the nest for ever. Stir me up, as the eagle stirs her nest, and teach me to fly.
Show me the burden You have given me, the gift You have put in my hand, and the ministry You have prepared for me.
Make our leaders servants who release rather than restrain, and make me a servant who can be trusted with freedom.
Let us do Your work in Your way, and pour out Your oil on all that we offer You. Amen.

The prophet then gave the widow a task that seemed absurd, to borrow every empty vessel and pour, and Evans believes church leaders should likewise help each member find a ministry that fits burden and gift. As she obeyed, the oil kept flowing. That, for him, is anointing: God setting His seal on obedient service, so that it bears fruit far beyond human ability, and the believer begins to soar. Releasing the eagles Much of the book is addressed to pastors and elders, and its counsel is practical. Evans suggests that every elders’ meeting should include two things: prayer to seek the mind of God, and a time to ask who in the congregation is ready to be released into ministry. Leaders should listen to people’s burdens, help them put them into words, seek confirmation of their gifts, and then give them room to serve, with clear authority, responsibility and accountability. As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God. 1 PETER 4:10 His stories include a man with a burden for prayer who, once released to teach it, helped a small congregation learn to wait on God and grow. Evans insists that releasing others is risky. They may fail and embarrass us; they may succeed and surpass us. Only leaders secure in their own calling can do it freely. God’s work in God’s way Evans returns often to the story of David bringing the ark to Jerusalem. The first attempt, on a new cart drawn by oxen, copied the method the Philistines had used, and ended in death. Only when David searched the law and had the Levites carry the ark on their shoulders, as Moses had commanded, did the presence of God come home with rejoicing. Much of the church, he fears, has borrowed the world’s methods of management, marketing and control, and wonders why the anointing is absent. Weighing the teaching Evans’s picture of the church as a place where every member is equipped and released is thoroughly biblical, and his warnings against controlling leadership are timely. Some of his applications may be weighed. His strong words about debt and about marriage to an unbeliever are pastoral warnings, not verdicts; he himself distinguishes a sensible mortgage from reckless borrowing, and Scripture is clear that God can greatly use a believer whose spouse does not yet believe. What burden has God laid on your heart? Try to describe it in a single clear sentence. 2. Ask two mature believers what gifts they see in you, and listen carefully. 3. Consider whether you have been waiting for someone else to carry a burden God has given to you. Take one step to begin. 4. If you lead in any way, think of one person you could release into ministry this year. Talk with them about their burden. 5. Look at one area of your church’s life and ask honestly whether it is being done God’s way or the world’s. A PRAYER Lord, You have not made me to sit in the nest for ever. Stir me up, as the eagle stirs her nest, and teach me to fly. Show me the burden You have given me, the gift You have put in my hand, and the ministry You have prepared for me. Make our leaders servants who release rather than restrain, and make me a servant who can be trusted with freedom. Let us do Your work in Your way, and pour out Your oil on all that we offer You. Amen.

fields.body_html:
And he said, I beseech thee, shew me thy glory. EXODUS 33:18

Evans is a Welshman, and Wales remembers the revival of 1904. His wife’s mother had been a girl in the village where it began; his first pastor’s father came to Christ in it. He grew up on its stories, and a longing for God to visit His people again has burned in him for seventy years. It is the theme of many of his sermons, among them Broken Before the Throne, Four Reasons We Need Revival in North America and Guard the Fire.

The awesome presence

What is revival? Evans tells of sitting with his brother-in-law and sister-in-law in Wales, both of whom had grown up among people converted in 1904, and asking them what had been so special about it. Was it the singing, the preaching, the healings? Both answered at once: it was the overwhelming sense that God Himself was present. That has become Evans’s own definition. Revival is God making His presence manifest among His people.

He is clear that revival is a sovereign act of God. No church can produce it by programmes, and not even by prayer, as though prayer were a lever. And yet Scripture sets out conditions, and he returns constantly to one verse:

If my people, which are called by my name, shall humble themselves, and pray, and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then will I hear from heaven, and will forgive their sin, and will heal their land. 2 CHRONICLES 7:14

The problem with our nations, Evans insists, is not first in their governments but in the church. God’s people must humble themselves and seek His face, not merely His hand. He adds unity, as Jesus prayed in John 17, and a hunger for God as strong as a drowning man’s hunger for air.

Moses, the calf and the tent

His fullest treatment is a sermon on Exodus 32 to 34. Moses came down the mountain to find Israel dancing round a golden calf. Evans draws several lessons. Sin must be dealt with radically; we have grown used to a God who shrugs at our failures, and have lost our sense of how terrible sin is in His presence. Moses identified himself with his people’s sin and interceded for them, offering to be blotted out of God’s book if they were not forgiven; so the church must stop pointing at the nation and confess its own failures.

Then God offered to send an angel before Israel instead of going Himself, and Moses refused.

And he said unto him, If thy presence go not with me, carry us not up hence. EXODUS 33:15

Evans asks whether churches have grown so used to being led by good men, good programmes and good organisation that they no longer need the Holy Spirit at all, and whether, if the Spirit withdrew, anything would change. When the people mourned, Moses pitched the tent of meeting outside the camp. Repentance, Evans says, must lead to separation, but true separation is not chiefly away from things. It is coming to Him, to the place of intimacy, just as Christ suffered outside the camp.

Standing on the rock

Moses’ prayer was the cry of a man who had already seen more of God than anyone alive: show me Thy glory. God answered that He knew Moses by name, and that He would proclaim His name before him.

And the LORD said, Behold, there is a place by me, and thou shalt stand upon a rock: and it shall come to pass, while my glory passeth by, that I will put thee in a clift of the rock, and will cover thee with my hand while I pass by. EXODUS 33:21–22

Evans takes the rock as a picture of Christ and the cross. Brokenness at the cross, he says, must come before any sight of the glory. People unwilling to die to themselves will never see God’s glory; at best they will admire their own. Then Moses was told to prepare himself and come up the mountain alone. Revival begins with individuals, prepared and presenting themselves to God.

Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully. PSALM 24:3–4

Why he longs for it

In one sermon Evans gives four reasons for his longing. He needs revival himself, daily. His church needs it, having grown so used to its own impotence that it thinks it normal. His nation needs it. And above all, the Saviour deserves it. He tells how, praying for his grandchildren, he realised that he wanted them saved partly for his own happiness, and how God showed him a better reason: that they should worship the One who is worthy. The same was true of revival. It is not finally about our experience. It is about the Lamb receiving the praise He is due.

Saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honour, and glory, and blessing. REVELATION 5:12

Another spirit

Evans loves Caleb, who at eighty-five asked Joshua for the mountain where the giants lived. God said of him that he had another spirit and had followed the Lord fully. Evans describes the seed of Caleb as worshippers, wholehearted, counter-cultural, renewed in youth like the eagle, hungry for fellowship with God, and willing to face giants, among them the giants of self. He preaches it as an old man who refuses to retire.

But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it. NUMBERS 14:24

Guard the fire

Finally, Evans pleads for the fire to be guarded. He asks worship leaders to lead people into the presence of the King, not merely to sing songs well, and reminds them that they must first have been in that presence themselves. He asks congregations to free their pastors to give themselves to prayer and the Word, as the apostles did in Acts 6. And he asks every believer to guard the fire God has lit, by prayer, by time alone with God, and by refusing to settle for less than His presence.

A reader may find some of his readings of Exodus, such as the distinction he draws between the two Hebrew words for rock, more ingenious than necessary, and his sermons occasionally touch on public events in a way he himself admits is speculative. But the heart of his plea is simply Scripture: God’s people are to seek His face until He comes.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself honestly whether your church would notice if the Holy Spirit withdrew. Pray about what you find.

2. Deal radically with one sin you have tolerated. Confess it and, where needed, remove whatever feeds it.

3. Set aside a regular time, however short, to seek God’s face rather than His hand.

4. Pray 2 Chronicles 7:14 for your church and your nation, beginning with yourself.

5. If you are older, ask God for Caleb’s mountain. If you are younger, find an older believer who still longs for God and learn from them.

A PRAYER
Lord God, I have seen something of Your goodness, and it has made me hungry for more. Show me Your glory.
I do not want an angel to lead us, or good men, or good programmes. If Your presence does not go with us, do not carry us up from here.
Break me before the cross, cleanse my hands and purify my heart, and begin in me the revival I long to see in Your church.
Not for my sake, Lord, but because the Lamb is worthy. Rend the heavens and come down. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:6

Fourteen chapters may make it look as though Gareth Evans teaches a great many things. In truth he teaches one thing, and applies it everywhere. God moves first, and the believer’s part is to take His hand and walk with Him.

Follow that thread back through the book and the shape appears. Faith is God’s own work in the heart, answered by obedience, and all its forms have their source in Him. The walk of faith is a child keeping hold of a Father’s hand, and hope is the settled expectation of all that Father has promised. God speaks quietly to those still enough to listen, and guides His children step by step, through closed doors and valleys. The believer who is in Christ is called to abide in Him and to feast on the riches that are his there, and to be filled with the Spirit whom the Father delights to give. God’s people are bound together by the covenant of the Upper Room: to serve, to love and to obey. When offence and old wounds break that fellowship, the key to healing is forgiveness, which God enables and which frees both the wounded and the one who wounded. Every believer has a burden, a gift and a ministry, and should be released to fly. And the church’s deepest need is not better methods but the manifest presence of God.

The danger of this book

If you have read this far, you are in some danger, and Evans would say so first. A teacher of stories and pictures is easily enjoyed and easily forgotten. It would be possible to finish these chapters having admired the apple tree, the eagle and the child holding its father’s hand, and to be exactly the same person as before.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

So the plainest counsel this book can give is the same as in its companion volumes. Go back to the chapter that made you least comfortable, not the one you enjoyed most. Take its application points and work them slowly over the coming months. If it was the chapter on offence, begin there. If it was the chapter on forgiveness, begin there, and take your time.

Two things to carry

Carry away, first, a settled rest. The Christian life is not an anxious search for a hidden plan, a strained effort to produce fruit, or a struggle to work up enough faith. It is a walk with a Father who has already acted, who holds your hand and who holds your future. You are asked to keep hold, to listen, to obey the next thing He shows you, and to trust Him for the rest.

Nevertheless I am continually with thee: thou hast holden me by my right hand. PSALM 73:23

Carry away, second, a holy hunger. Evans has never been content with a quiet, comfortable Christianity. He wants believers to fly, churches to be places where God is known to be present, and the Lamb to receive the worship He deserves. Rest and hunger are not opposites. The one who rests in God is the one who can hunger for more of Him without anxiety.

A last word about the man

We have been honest in these pages about the places where Evans’s teaching should be weighed. His distinctions between faith, hope and belief are sharper than the New Testament’s vocabulary; some of his word studies and Old Testament pictures read more into the text than it requires; his understanding of the baptism in the Spirit and of binding and loosing is one view among several held by faithful Christians; and his many stories of remarkable providence are testimonies, not templates for every life. None of this has been said to diminish him. He himself warns against building doctrine on experience and against taking one verse and building a following on it, and he would want his readers to test him by the same rule.

What remains is a life that has matched its teaching. A physics teacher who left a large salary because he believed God had called him; a pastor who shared the credit for his churches’ growth with the people he released; a chaplain who taught pastors in West Africa; a husband who gives his wife the praise others have given him; an old man who has taken to the streets of his city because he believes that only Jesus is the answer to what he finds there. He has walked, as far as any of us can tell, with the One he taught others to walk with.

The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage. PSALM 16:6
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Return to the chapter of this book that made you least comfortable. Choose one application point and work on it for a month.

2. Ask whether anything in these pages has become a new burden or law to you. If so, bring it to God and receive it again as grace.

3. Name one way you will keep hold of the Father’s hand each day, whether a morning prayer, a walk alone with God or a pause before work.

4. Choose one person to forgive, one person to encourage and one person to help release into their calling.

5. Begin one of Evans’s own books from the Reader’s Guide that follows.

A PRAYER
Father, I have read about faith and hope, about abiding and forgiving, about gifts and glory, and I am capable of leaving it all on the page. Do not let me.
Hold my hand today. Let me hear Your voice, obey the next thing You show me, and trust You with the rest.
Heal what is wounded in me, loose me from bitterness, and release me into the work You have prepared.
And as You have been faithful to Your servant through a long life, be faithful to me, until the walk is ended and I see You face to face. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to Gareth Evans
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Evans is easy to read and, for Ochorus readers, easy to find. All five of his books are shared free in the Ochorus library with his permission, and eleven of his sermons, transcribed from recordings, are there by his permission too. He writes as he speaks: plainly, warmly, with many stories, and with the instincts of a schoolteacher who wants to be understood. His books are short, and none requires a theological education.

Begin here

He Holds My Tomorrows. His book on faith, and the natural place to start. It clears away common misunderstandings, sets out the three kinds of faith he finds in Scripture, and then walks through the people of Hebrews 11 as examples of God’s leading. Chapters three to seven of this volume draw chiefly on it. In the Ochorus library.

The Key in My Hand. His best-known book, on the covenant of the Upper Room, the body of Christ, offence, the wounded soul, and healing through forgiveness and release. Read it slowly, and alongside the cautions in chapter fourteen of this volume. If it opens old wounds, find someone to walk with you. In the Ochorus library.

For the whole story

Stepping Stones. His autobiography, from the Welsh valleys through classrooms, pastorates and the Mercy Ship to his later ministry, told as a series of stepping stones laid by God. It is also a book about guidance, and chapter eight of this volume draws on it. It is the only book-length account of his life; the Ochorus author page carries a shorter biography. In the Ochorus library.

For those who serve

Soar Like the Eagle. On why so many believers never fly, and how burden, gifting, ministry and anointing belong together. Much of it is addressed to pastors and elders, with practical counsel on releasing people into ministry. The basis of chapter fifteen of this volume. In the Ochorus library.

Feasting at the Table. A short study of Ephesians, drawn from lectures at a Bible school summer school: Paul’s prayers, the riches of being in Christ, the body and the building, the Christian walk and standing firm. The basis of chapter ten of this volume, and a good companion to reading Ephesians itself. In the Ochorus library.

His sermons

The sermons on Ochorus are transcriptions of spoken messages, preached over some twenty years, and they have the directness and repetition of the pulpit. Faith is the best companion to his book on the subject. Abiding in Christ, The Glory of His Inheritance, Burdens and Gifts and Caleb: A Different Spirit are short and pastoral. Broken Before the Throne and Four Reasons We Need Revival in North America carry his longing for revival, and the three messages Guard the Truth, Guard the Gift and Guard the Fire, preached as a series in his late eighties, are perhaps the best single introduction to the man. Mary of Bethany is a brief meditation. Evans maintains his own website as well, where further devotional writing can be found.

Approach with care

Nothing he has written is dangerous, but a few emphases need the balance supplied in this volume: the sharpness of his distinctions between faith, hope and belief (chapter three); his reading of the baptism in the Spirit (chapter eleven); his linking of some sickness with broken relationships (chapter twelve); his reading of Mary of Bethany’s grief (chapter thirteen); and his interpretation of binding, loosing and releasing (chapter fourteen). Read these with the Bible open.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him for the stories, and then ask what the story teaches. Evans is at his best when a single incident, a stammering young man, a prayer meeting, a closed door, illuminates a principle of Scripture. The story will stay with you; make sure the principle does too.

Read him with the Bible open. He constantly sends his readers to the text, and his books are full of references to look up. Do so.

And read him as he would want to be read: with a view to obeying. He has little interest in readers who enjoy his teaching and do nothing with it. Take one thing from each chapter and act on it.

The path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day. PROVERBS 4:18
fields.body_text: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15 Evans is easy to read and, for Ochorus readers, easy to find. All five of his books are shared free in the Ochorus library with his permission, and eleven of his sermons, transcribed from recordings, are there by his permission too. He writes as he speaks: plainly, warmly, with many stories, and with the instincts of a schoolteacher who wants to be understood. His books are short, and none requires a theological education. Begin here He Holds My Tomorrows. His book on faith, and the natural place to start. It clears away common misunderstandings, sets out the three kinds of faith he finds in Scripture, and then walks through the people of Hebrews 11 as examples of God’s leading. Chapters three to seven of this volume draw chiefly on it. In the Ochorus library. The Key in My Hand. His best-known book, on the covenant of the Upper Room, the body of Christ, offence, the wounded soul, and healing through forgiveness and release. Read it slowly, and alongside the cautions in chapter fourteen of this volume. If it opens old wounds, find someone to walk with you. In the Ochorus library. For the whole story Stepping Stones. His autobiography, from the Welsh valleys through classrooms, pastorates and the Mercy Ship to his later ministry, told as a series of stepping stones laid by God. It is also a book about guidance, and chapter eight of this volume draws on it. It is the only book-length account of his life; the Ochorus author page carries a shorter biography. In the Ochorus library. For those who serve Soar Like the Eagle. On why so many believers never fly, and how burden, gifting, ministry and anointing belong together. Much of it is addressed to pastors and elders, with practical counsel on releasing people into ministry. The basis of chapter fifteen of this volume. In the Ochorus library. Feasting at the Table. A short study of Ephesians, drawn from lectures at a Bible school summer school: Paul’s prayers, the riches of being in Christ, the body and the building, the Christian walk and standing firm. The basis of chapter ten of this volume, and a good companion to reading Ephesians itself. In the Ochorus library. His sermons The sermons on Ochorus are transcriptions of spoken messages, preached over some twenty years, and they have the directness and repetition of the pulpit. Faith is the best companion to his book on the subject. Abiding in Christ, The Glory of His Inheritance, Burdens and Gifts and Caleb: A Different Spirit are short and pastoral. Broken Before the Throne and Four Reasons We Need Revival in North America carry his longing for revival, and the three messages Guard the Truth, Guard the Gift and Guard the Fire, preached as a series in his late eighties, are perhaps the best single introduction to the man. Mary of Bethany is a brief meditation. Evans maintains his own website as well, where further devotional writing can be found. Approach with care Nothing he has written is dangerous, but a few emphases need the balance supplied in this volume: the sharpness of his distinctions between faith, hope and belief (chapter three); his reading of the baptism in the Spirit (chapter eleven); his linking of some sickness with broken relationships (chapter twelve); his reading of Mary of Bethany’s grief (chapter thirteen); and his interpretation of binding, loosing and releasing (chapter fourteen).
